mappings.rationale: Requires a board-approved, periodically reviewed Internet Banking security framework document with defined BOD/management/employee roles — the definition-approval-review lifecycle of 5.1 plus the role allocation of 5.2 and management ownership of 5.4.

The stated objective is that systems are free from unauthorized access and customer information is not modified, which is the access-control policy objective of 5.15 stated as a goal rather than an implemented control.
Confidentiality of customer data specifically at rest, in processing and in transit is achieved in ISO 27002 by cryptographic protection (8.24) and by secured transfer channels (5.14).
Availability and prompt access to Internet Banking systems maps to ICT continuity readiness (5.30) and to the redundancy of processing facilities that delivers required availability (8.14).
Traceability of every transaction is delivered by transaction logging (8.15), and the objective explicitly requires SOPs to achieve it (5.37).
Proactive detection of unauthorized access and identification of anomalous/fraudulent transactions is exactly the anomalous-behaviour monitoring required by 8.16.

Conducting, documenting and annually re-performing a security risk assessment is an ISMS management-process requirement (ISO 27001 clause 6.1.2/8.2), not an ISO 27002 control — 27002 contains no risk-assessment control to map to.
Requires a current documented description of systems and the locations/methods holding customer information, which is the asset and information inventory of 5.9 applied as a risk-assessment input.
Identifying the information and information systems to be protected is verbatim the identification of information and associated assets required by 5.9.
Ranking sensitive systems, payment data and applications high/medium/low by importance is information classification per 5.12.

Assessing threats and vulnerabilities to systems and payment data corresponds to technical vulnerability identification (8.8) informed by threat information (5.7), though SBP frames it as a risk-assessment input rather than an operational process.
ISO 27002 has no fraud or identity-theft control; the only related theme is the identity lifecycle assurance of 5.16, so this is a thematic link only.

Evaluating effectiveness of existing controls against each threat is closest to the independent review of the information security approach in 5.35, but SBP requires it as part of self-performed risk assessment rather than an independent review.
Defining security and contractual responsibilities of service providers with access to bank systems and data is precisely the agreement content required by 5.20.
Assessing compliance, concentration, operational, country and legal risk before entering and while managing outsourcing arrangements is the supplier-relationship risk process of 5.19.
Requires assessment of the bank's obligations under named sections of the Payment Systems and EFT Act 2007, which is the identification of legal/statutory requirements in 5.31.

Mandates a minimum baseline of access rights management, OS access, application access, remote and network access controls — 5.15 for the access-control rule set, 8.3 for application/data access restriction, 8.20 for network access.
Section heading introducing the mandatory customer authentication control set, matching secure authentication (8.5) and the handling of authentication credentials (5.17).
Registration/enrollment of Internet Banking customers only after due verification is the identity proofing and registration step of the identity lifecycle in 5.16.
Mandatory two-factor authentication (password plus one-time token/dongle) is the strong authentication technique explicitly required by 8.5.
Additional layered authentication for high-value transactions is the risk-based step-up authentication contemplated by 8.5, though the transaction-value trigger is banking-specific.
Failed log-in attempt limits, session timeout and re-authentication are the log-on control behaviours of 8.5; mandated password change frequency is credential management under 5.17.

Periodic re-assessment of authentication controls against changing threats and breach history shares only its subject matter with 8.5; the reassessment cycle itself is an ISO 27001 management-process requirement.
Heading scoping the following controls to bank employees using Internet Banking systems; only the general access-control rule-setting of 5.15 corresponds, with the substance in its sub-requirements.

Access rights matched to job function, authorized before change, periodically reviewed and least-privilege enforced is the provisioning/review cycle of 5.18, with least privilege over sensitive systems covered by 8.2.
Restricting, regularly monitoring and auditing privileged operating-system access is the privileged access rights control 8.2, with the monitoring obligation in 8.16.

Remote access to high-risk assets requiring written management approval, strong authentication and encrypted communications matches the remote-working security measures of 6.7 and the strong authentication requirement of 8.5.
Restricting physical access to systems, segments and data sites and logging/monitoring it is the physical entry control 7.2 combined with the surveillance and logging of 7.4.
Securing IT networks through multiple layers of controls is the layered network security of 8.20, with the layering between zones realised through network segregation (8.22).
Firewalls deployed between security domains to control traffic per network risk classification is the gateway-enforced network segregation of 8.22 within the network security management of 8.20.
IDS/IPS deployed between security domains is the intrusion-detection tooling named in 8.16, applied to network traffic managed under 8.20.

ISO 27002 has no identity-theft/fraud-prevention control; the programme's identity-assurance element touches 5.16 and its protection of customer identity data touches 5.34, so the link is thematic only.
Requires reliable encryption for access, storage and data communication of sensitive payment data — the cryptographic use control 8.24.
Maintaining traceability of executed transactions to discharge statutory burden-of-proof obligations is transaction logging (8.15) plus the retention and integrity of those records (5.33).
Regular employee training on security risks, controls, monitoring mechanisms and policy changes is the awareness, education and training control 6.3.

Contractually binding service providers to these security regulations while the bank retains accountability is the supplier relationship policy of 5.19 implemented through the agreement requirements of 5.20.
Requires non-disclosure provisions and bank/SBP right-to-audit clauses in service provider contracts — NDA terms per 6.6 embedded in supplier agreements per 5.20.
Requires service providers to implement measures preventing loss, theft or leakage of customer information, i.e. data leakage prevention (8.12) imposed as a supplier agreement obligation (5.20).

Service provider access to customer information must be request-triggered, strictly monitored, logged and periodically audited with no transfer to unauthorized media — supplier service monitoring/review (5.22) over a restricted access path (8.3).
Requires service providers to hold DR plans, DR site tiers and asset lifecycle documentation — ICT continuity readiness (5.30) imposed on the supplier under the supplier relationship control (5.19).
A disaster recovery plan aligned to the bank's business requirements is ICT readiness for business continuity based on business-derived recovery objectives (5.30).
Maintaining cold/warm/hot/satellite recovery sites is the provision of redundant information processing facilities in 8.14.
Documentation of IT asset life cycle management at the service provider is the maintained asset inventory and ownership record of 5.9.
A formally approved mechanism for monitoring security controls, including analysis of monitoring method effectiveness, is the establishment of monitoring activities under 8.16.
Collecting and analysing host and network data on security events such as privileged access, configuration changes and critical application access is monitoring (8.16) fed by event logs (8.15).
Nominating a rapid response team and documenting breach response methods is the incident response structure and responsibilities of 5.24, driven by proactive IDS/IPS monitoring (8.16).
Monitoring and reporting on authentication controls maps to 8.16, and the requirement that it be formally documented and approved by senior management maps to management responsibilities in 5.4.
Defining system restoration procedures and restoration times is the recovery-time/procedure element of ICT continuity readiness (5.30), operationally supported by backup restoration (8.13).
Self-assessments and independent security audits are the independent review of 5.35, and penetration testing is the vulnerability identification technique required by 8.8.
Identifying policy violations is the compliance verification of 5.36, and detecting unauthorized configuration changes is the configuration monitoring/drift detection required by 8.9.
Regular periodic review of logs and audit trails is 8.15, and the mandated ten-year retention of those security logs is protection and retention of records under 5.33.

A formal awareness programme on Internet Banking threats and safeguards matches 6.3, which extends awareness obligations to relevant interested parties, though ISO frames it around personnel rather than retail customers.

Explaining respective liabilities and responsibilities of bank and customer is a consumer-disclosure obligation; only the act of communicating security responsibilities to an interested party touches 6.3.
Compliance with the Section 30 disclosure requirements of the Payment Systems and EFT Act 2007 is the identification and meeting of a specific statutory requirement under 5.31.
Publishing help desk contact details for reporting lost credentials, fraud or identity theft is the security event reporting channel of 6.8 and the point-of-contact preparation required by 5.24.
A defined procedure for re-authenticating Internet Banking customers is a log-on/authentication procedure under 8.5, here communicated to customers as awareness material.

Customer complaint handling and dispute resolution for banking transactions is a consumer-protection and financial-redress obligation with no counterpart in ISO 27002, whose incident controls address security events, not customer disputes.
Yearly re-issuance of risk-mitigation guidelines to customers is the periodic refresh of awareness material required by 6.3.
Management review and evaluation of the awareness programme matches the evaluation of awareness effectiveness in 6.3 and management's ownership of security promotion in 5.4.

Mandatory quarterly submission of established security breach reports to the SBP Payment Systems Department is reporting to a regulatory authority under 5.5, discharged as a statutory obligation under 5.31.
States the regulations operate subject to all other SBP laws, rules and circulars — the identification and tracking of applicable regulatory requirements in 5.31.
Compliance with the SBP Outsourcing Arrangements circular is a regulatory obligation (5.31) whose subject matter is supplier/outsourcing security governance (5.19).
Compliance with the SBP IT Security Guidelines circular is a regulatory obligation (5.31) requiring the bank's security policy set to reflect that external standard (5.1).
The referenced circular covers information systems audits (independent review, 5.35) and system switchover planning (ICT readiness for continuity, 5.30).
Compliance with the SBP Business Continuity Planning guidelines maps to maintaining information security during disruption (5.29) and the ICT continuity capability that supports it (5.30).
The quarterly template compels reporting breach details to the regulator (5.5) and its columns for breach cause, impact and rectifying action capture the lessons-learned analysis of 5.27.
